title: Where Wisdom Comes From
sum: The book opens with the grandson's prologue, written in Greek in Egypt. He explains who wrote the book (his grandfather Jesus, a student of the law, the prophets and the other books), why he translated it (so that Jews abroad who love learning can live by the law), and why a translation never quite matches the Hebrew.

Chapter 1 then sets the theme of the whole book. All wisdom comes from the Lord, who created Wisdom first of all things and poured her out on all his works. People receive her through the fear of the Lord, which Ben Sira praises in a little hymn (1:11–20): it is glory, joy, long life, the beginning, fullness, crown and root of wisdom. The chapter ends with warnings: anger and pride bring a fall; the one who wants wisdom must keep the commandments and must not come to God with a double heart.
readings: Read as a hymn to God's Wisdom

Chapter 1 belongs with Proverbs 8, Job 28 and Baruch 3:9–4:4: poems in which Wisdom is God's first creation, hidden from human searching but given to those who love him. Read this way, the chapter is about God before it is about us.
Read as the teacher's opening lesson

Ben Sira is a schoolmaster, and chapter 1 states his program: wisdom is not clever technique but the fear of the Lord and obedience to the law (1:26–27). Everything that follows, on parents, money, speech and friends, applies that rule.

views.C: The Catholic Church reads 1:1–10 at Mass on a weekday of the seventh week in Ordinary Time. The Latin Vulgate, its Bible for centuries, adds that God created Wisdom "in the Holy Spirit" (Vulgate 1:9; Douay "in the Holy Ghost"), a phrase not in the Greek.
views.O: The Orthodox churches read this chapter in the Greek form translated here, as part of their Old Testament. For the question whether Wisdom "created" can be said of Christ, see the card at Proverbs 8.
views.P: For Protestants the book is not Scripture, but the chapter's teaching matches Proverbs and Job: wisdom is God's gift, and its beginning is the fear of the Lord. Protestant readers value the grandson's prologue as an early witness to the three-part Hebrew Bible, the canon Protestant Old Testaments follow.
views.H: Historians date Ben Sira's book to about 180 BC and the grandson's arrival in Egypt to 132 BC. Many read chapter 1 as a claim made in an age of Greek learning: true wisdom is the gift of Israel's God, found in the fear of the Lord and the law.
views.J: Ben Sira is not in the Jewish Bible, but the chapter's thought, that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom and that wisdom comes through the commandments, is the thought of Proverbs and of later Jewish teaching that identified Wisdom with the Torah.

deep.h: The prologue and the shape of the Bible
deep.b: The grandson's prologue names Israel's books three times, each time in three groups: the law, the prophets, and "the others" or "the rest of the books." That matches the three parts of the Jewish Bible (Torah, Prophets, Writings) and is usually counted as the earliest witness to them. He also says that the law and the prophets were already read in translation, that is, in Greek. Two cautions apply. He never names the third group, and he never lists its books, so the prologue shows a recognized collection but not its exact contents. And he says plainly that his own Greek does not match the Hebrew: "Words spoken in Hebrew do not carry the same force when they are carried over into another language." Where the Hebrew of Ben Sira survives, from 3:6 on in this part, the site's variant notes show how often the grandson changed a word or a picture.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the prologue's "copy" is the book itself
deep.b: The grandson says he "found" something in Egypt (aphomoion, a likeness or copy) and then at once judged it necessary to translate "this book." The simplest reading is that the family's Hebrew book had reached Egypt before him, perhaps carried by other Jews from Jerusalem, and that finding it there, among Greek-speaking Jews who could not read it, is what moved him. If so, the prologue gives a rare glimpse of a Hebrew book traveling to the dispersion before it was translated. Scholars have taken the word in other ways, and this reading rests only on the order of the grandson's sentences.

echoes: Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 2:6; Proverbs 8:22–31; Proverbs 9:10; Job 28:12–28; Baruch 3:29–4:4; Psalm 111:10; Luke 24:44; Romans 11:33; Romans 16:27; James 1:5; Matthew 6:2–5; Luke 14:11

settings.by: Ben Sira's grandson, who does not give his own name
settings.to: Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt and elsewhere in the dispersion who "love learning"
settings.when: after he arrived in Egypt in the thirty-eighth year of Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II (132 BC)
settings.why: To present his grandfather's Hebrew book in Greek, to explain that it is meant to help readers "live by the law," and to ask pardon for a translation that cannot match the Hebrew. It also tells the reader that the book stands in the line of the law, the prophets and the other books, though it is not one of them.
settings.readers: Jews of the dispersion, chiefly in Egypt, after 132 BC. Through the Greek Bible the book later passed to the Christian churches, which copied it in the great codices (Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus).

settings.what: Opening poem: Wisdom, the fear of the Lord, and warnings
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Sirach), a Jerusalem teacher of wisdom
settings.to: his pupils, and any reader who wants wisdom
settings.when: in Jerusalem, about 190–180 BC, as the opening of his book
settings.why: To set out the foundation of everything he will teach: wisdom is God's gift, it is received through the fear of the Lord, and it is kept by keeping the commandments. The closing warnings (1:22–30) show that the fear of the Lord is practical: it rules anger, speech and pride.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were the young men of a Jerusalem school of wisdom about 190–180 BC, from families who could expect to hold office (4:7–9). After 132 BC the grandson's Greek served Jews in Egypt, and the Hebrew kept being copied: a fragment at Qumran (2Q18, 6:14–31) and the medieval copies found in the Cairo Genizah.

title: Ready to Be Tested
sum: "My child, if you step forward to be a servant of the Lord God, make your soul ready for testing." The chapter is Ben Sira's lesson on hardship. Trials will come; the faithful accept them as gold accepts the furnace, and wait for God's mercy.

Three sayings addressed to "you who fear the Lord" (2:7–9) call for waiting, trust and hope; history shows that no one who trusted the Lord was left alone (2:10), for the Lord is full of pity and mercy (2:11). Three woes (2:12–14) fall on the timid, the double-minded and those who give up. Three promises (2:15–17) describe those who fear the Lord. The chapter ends with David's choice: better to fall into the Lord's hands than into human hands (2:18).
readings: Read as encouragement
For pupils about to take up adult lives, the chapter says that hardship is not a sign that God has left them. It is part of serving him, and it proves faith as fire proves gold.
Read beside the New Testament

James 1:2–4 and 1 Peter 1:6–7 say much the same: trials prove faith and produce endurance. Christian readers have heard the chapter as a preparation for the sufferings of Christ's followers (2 Timothy 3:12).

views.C: The Catholic lectionary reads 2:1–11 on a weekday of the seventh week in Ordinary Time, and 2:7–13 for Saint Cajetan (August 7) and in the Common of Holy Men and Women. The Latin adds "If we do not do penance" before the saying of 2:18 (Vulgate 2:22, Douay).
views.O: The Orthodox churches read the chapter in its Greek form, in which the beginner serves "the Lord God" (2:1). Its counsel on trials stands close to James 1:2–4 and 1 Peter 1:6–7, which every church reads.
views.P: Protestant readers find the chapter's counsel close to James and 1 Peter, and value it as wisdom; they hold that trials refine faith but do not earn God's favor.
views.H: Scholars note the chapter's careful structure (three and three) and its teaching style, and set it in the strains of Jerusalem in the early 100s BC, when loyalty to the law could cost a man position and wealth.
views.J: The chapter's trust in God's mercy echoes Exodus 34:6 and Psalm 22:5; the saying of 2:18 takes up David's words in 2 Samuel 24:14.

echoes: James 1:2–4; James 1:12; James 5:11; 1 Peter 1:6–7; Proverbs 17:3; Wisdom of Solomon 3:6; Exodus 34:6; Psalm 22:4–5; 1 Kings 18:21; Matthew 6:24; 2 Samuel 24:14; Hebrews 10:31

settings.what: A lesson on testing and trust
settings.to: "my child," a pupil about to commit himself to serving the Lord
settings.when: in Ben Sira's school in Jerusalem, about 190–180 BC
settings.why: To prepare the pupil for hardship: serving God brings trials, which prove and refine; trust and hope in God's mercy carry him through, while timidity and divided loyalty ruin him.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were the young men of a Jerusalem school of wisdom about 190–180 BC, from families who could expect to hold office (4:7–9). After 132 BC the grandson's Greek served Jews in Egypt, and the Hebrew kept being copied: a fragment at Qumran (2Q18, 6:14–31) and the medieval copies found in the Cairo Genizah.

title: Honor, Humility and Alms
sum: Ben Sira expands the fifth commandment into a sermon (3:1–16): the one who honors father and mother atones for sins, stores up treasure, is heard in prayer and lives long. Grown sons must care for aging fathers, even when their minds fail; kindness to a father will be remembered in place of sins. Whoever abandons his father is like a blasphemer.

Then come humility (3:17–20): the greater you are, the lower you should make yourself. Do not pry into things too hard for you (3:21–24); the hard heart and the proud man come to ruin (3:26–28). The chapter ends with one of Ben Sira's best-known sayings: as water puts out fire, alms atone for sins (3:30). From 3:6 on, the Hebrew survives in a medieval copy from the Cairo Genizah.
readings: Read as family ethics
Ben Sira speaks to sons who will soon head households while their parents grow old. Honor means practical care, patience and respect, not only obedience in childhood.
Read as teaching on sin and atonement

Twice the chapter says that good deeds "atone for sins" (3:3, 30). Jewish readers have heard this as a call to repentance in deed; churches differ on whether such deeds take away sin, and the cards at Tobit 4 and Proverbs 16 set out their answers.

views.C: The Catechism quotes 3:2–6, 12–13 and 16 on the duties of grown children toward their parents (2218), and the lectionary reads 3:2–6 and 3:12–14 on the Feast of the Holy Family and 3:17–20, 28–29 on the 22nd Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year C). Catholic teaching joins almsgiving with prayer and fasting as works of penance.
views.O: The Orthodox churches read the chapter in its Greek form. On almsgiving and sin, the card at Tobit 4 gives the Orthodox view from John Chrysostom: alms are a remedy for sin within a life of repentance, not a payment.
views.P: Protestants honor the chapter's teaching on parents and humility, but deny that honoring parents or giving alms atones for sin: forgiveness comes through Christ alone, and good works are its fruit.
views.H: The Hebrew of manuscript A (from 3:6) often differs from the Greek: a garden picture for houses (3:9), "provokes his Creator" (3:16), humility for the rich (3:17), the mocker's wound (3:28), and tsedaqah, "righteousness," for alms (3:30). Scholars see in the passage on hidden things (3:21–24) a warning against speculation.
views.J: The Talmud quotes 3:21–22 in Hebrew from "the book of Ben Sira" (Hagigah 13a). The teaching that tsedaqah atones (3:30) became central in Jewish ethics, where giving to the poor is called by the same word as righteousness.

deep.h: Does doing good atone for sin?
deep.b: Ben Sira says it twice: "The one who honors a father makes atonement for sins" (3:3), and "sins are atoned for by alms" (3:30). He uses the temple's word for atonement (Greek exilaskomai, Hebrew kipper in 3:30). He is not alone. Proverbs 16:6 says guilt is atoned for by loyal love and faithfulness, Daniel 4:27 tells a king to break with his sins by mercy to the poor, and Tobit 12:9 says alms cleanse away every sin. Ben Sira also guards against misuse: do not say God's mercy will cover sins you keep committing (5:4–6). Jewish tradition kept the teaching as part of repentance. Churches differ: Catholic and Orthodox teaching gives almsgiving a place in repentance and healing from sin, always by God's grace, while Protestant teaching holds that only Christ's sacrifice atones and that good works follow forgiveness. The full answers, with their sources, are on the cards at Tobit 4 and Proverbs 16.

settings.to: "children": his pupils, young men who would soon care for aging parents
settings.when: in Ben Sira's school in Jerusalem, about 190–180 BC
settings.why: To apply the fifth commandment to adult life: honor parents in word and deed, care for them in old age, bear with them when their minds fail. The promised rewards (atonement, answered prayer, long life, blessing) urge the pupils to keep it when it costs them.

settings.what: Instruction on humility, curiosity, the hard heart and alms
settings.to: "my child": a pupil, in the Hebrew one who is or will be rich (3:17)
settings.when: in Ben Sira's school, about 190–180 BC
settings.why: To teach the powerful to make themselves low, to leave hidden things to God and keep to the law they have been shown, and to give to the poor. Knowing the pupils were from leading families, the warnings against pride and the praise of alms speak to their temptations.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were the young men of a Jerusalem school of wisdom about 190–180 BC, from families who could expect to hold office (4:7–9). After 132 BC the grandson's Greek served Jews in Egypt, and the Hebrew kept being copied: a fragment at Qumran (2Q18, 6:14–31) and the medieval copies found in the Cairo Genizah.

title: Wisdom's Hard School
sum: Ben Sira turns to the poor (4:1–10): do not rob them, keep them waiting, turn your face from them, or give them cause to curse you, for their Maker hears. Rescue the wronged; be a father to orphans and a husband to their mother, and you will be like a son of the Most High.

Then Wisdom appears as a mother and teacher (4:11–19). Those who love her love life; those who serve her serve the Holy One. But she tests her pupils first by crooked ways, fear and discipline, until she can trust them; then she returns and shows them her secrets. The chapter ends with a little essay on right and wrong shame (4:20–28) and advice for the master of a house (4:29–31).
readings: Read as social ethics

The chapter speaks to future officials and householders: justice for the poor, courage as a judge, respect without flattery, gentleness at home. Its concern for orphans and widows runs from Deuteronomy to James 1:27.
Read as the way of a disciple

Wisdom's school (4:17–18) has the pattern of discipleship: testing first, then trust and revelation. Christian readers have compared it to the way Jesus formed his disciples, and Jewish readers to the study of Torah.

views.C: The lectionary reads 4:11–19 on a weekday of the seventh week in Ordinary Time. The Latin of 4:26 (Vulgate 4:31) keeps "confess," and the Douay has "Be not ashamed to confess thy sins." On confession to a priest, see the card at Psalm 32.
views.O: The Orthodox churches read the Greek "confess" in 4:26; on confession to a priest, see the card at Psalm 32.
views.P: Protestant readers find the teaching on the poor and on justice close to the prophets and James. They read 4:26 as confession to God, with or without a pastor.
views.H: The Hebrew of manuscript A differs often: it has "mock" for "rob" in 4:1, God calling the merciful man his son in 4:10, Wisdom speaking in the first person in 4:15–19, "truth" for "nations" in 4:15, "turn" for "confess" in 4:26, and "a dog" for "a lion" in 4:30.
views.J: The chapter's care for the poor matches the law (Exodus 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 24:14–15). The Hebrew has Wisdom speak as a teacher who disguises herself to test her student, a picture close to later Jewish ideas of learning Torah.

echoes: Deuteronomy 24:14–15; Exodus 22:22–24; Proverbs 14:31; Psalm 68:5; Luke 6:35; James 1:27; Proverbs 8:32–36; Luke 7:35; Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–11; Leviticus 19:15; James 2:1; James 5:16; 1 John 1:9; Exodus 14:14; Didache 4:5; Acts 20:35

settings.what: Instruction on the poor, the wronged and the orphan
settings.to: "my child": pupils who would have wealth and some would sit as judges (4:9)
settings.when: in Ben Sira's school, about 190–180 BC
settings.why: To bind the future powerful to the law's care for the poor: pay promptly, give, listen, rescue, and protect orphans and widows. God hears the poor man's cry, so cruelty to him is defiance of God.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were the young men of a Jerusalem school of wisdom about 190–180 BC, from families who could expect to hold office (4:7–9). settings.by: Ben Sira; in the Hebrew Wisdom herself speaks from 4:15
settings.when: in Ben Sira's school, about 190–180 BC
settings.why: To prepare the pupil for the hard beginning of study: Wisdom tests before she trusts. The promise of joy, glory and her secrets keeps him going.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were the young men of a Jerusalem school of wisdom about 190–180 BC, from families who could expect to hold office (4:7–9). settings.what: Sayings on shame, truth and the household
settings.when: in Ben Sira's school, about 190–180 BC
settings.why: To teach a balanced sense of shame (ashamed of sin and ignorance, never of right or of confessing sins), courage for the truth, and gentleness as master of a house.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were the young men of a Jerusalem school of wisdom about 190–180 BC, from families who could expect to hold office (4:7–9). title: Do Not Presume
sum: A chain of "Do not" sayings. Do not lean on wealth or say, "It is enough for me"; do not follow your desires or say, "Who can lord it over me?" (5:1–3). Above all, do not presume on God's mercy: do not say, "I sinned, and what did it do to me?" or "His pity is great; it will atone for my sins," for mercy and anger are both with him. Do not put off turning to the Lord (5:4–7).

Then speech (5:9–15): do not winnow with every wind; be firm, be quick to listen and slow to answer, speak only when you understand. The tongue brings honor or shame; the double-tongued sinner earns a bitter verdict. The last sentence runs over into chapter 6.
readings: Read as a warning against false security
Wealth, strength and even God's mercy can become excuses. Ben Sira's pupil is warned against each of them, with the urgency of 5:7: today, not tomorrow.
Read as a guide to speech
The second half belongs with James 1:19 and James 3: listen first, keep your word single, and remember that the tongue can bring a man down.

views.C: The lectionary reads 5:1–8 on a weekday of the seventh week in Ordinary Time, under the heading "Delay not your conversion to the Lord," from the Latin of 5:7.
views.O: The Orthodox churches read the chapter in its Greek form, in which 5:5–6 speak of "atonement" where the Hebrew has "forgiveness."
views.P: Protestant readers hear 5:4–7 alongside Romans 2:4 and 6:1: God's patience leads to repentance, and grace is no license to sin.
views.H: The Hebrew of manuscript A survives for the whole chapter and differs in places: an idiom of power in 5:1 (as in Genesis 31:29), God who seeks the pursued in 5:3 (as in Ecclesiastes 3:15), "forgiveness" for "atonement" in 5:5, and "false riches" in 5:8.
views.J: The chapter's teaching on repentance (teshuvah, "turning") and on not relying on God's forgiveness while continuing to sin is close to later rabbinic teaching on repentance.

echoes: Proverbs 11:28; Psalm 49:6; Luke 12:15–21; Ecclesiastes 8:11; Romans 2:4–5; Romans 6:1; Exodus 34:6–7; Romans 11:22; Hebrews 3:13; 2 Corinthians 6:2; Proverbs 10:2; Luke 16:9; Ephesians 4:14; Matthew 5:37; James 1:19; James 3:2–10; Romans 1:29

settings.what: Warnings against trusting wealth and presuming on mercy
settings.to: the pupil, a young man likely to have wealth and power
settings.when: in Ben Sira's school, about 190–180 BC
settings.why: To strip away false securities: money, strength and a lazy trust that God will forgive whatever one does. The point is to make the pupil turn to the Lord now.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were the young men of a Jerusalem school of wisdom about 190–180 BC, from families who could expect to hold office (4:7–9). After 132 BC the grandson's Greek served Jews in Egypt, and the Hebrew kept being copied: a fragment at Qumran (2Q18, 6:14–31) and the medieval copies found in the Cairo Genizah.

settings.what: Sayings on steady and honest speech
settings.when: in Ben Sira's school, about 190–180 BC
settings.why: To train a man for public life: listen first, answer only with understanding, keep one word, and never be two-faced.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were the young men of a Jerusalem school of wisdom about 190–180 BC, from families who could expect to hold office (4:7–9). title: Friends, and Wisdom's Yoke
sum: After a warning about desire that devours a man like a stripped tree (6:2–4), Ben Sira gives his famous teaching on friendship (6:5–17). Kind speech wins friends, but test a friend before you trust him: some are friends only in good times, some turn into enemies, some share your table and vanish in trouble. "A faithful friend is a solid roof over you"; he is beyond price, "a medicine that gives life," and those who fear the Lord will find such a friend.

Then Ben Sira calls the young to seek Wisdom (6:18–37). She is like a field to plow, a heavy stone the fool soon throws off, a yoke with fetters and a collar. But the fetters become a shelter, the collar a robe of glory, the ropes royal blue. Stand among the elders, cling to the wise, wear out their doorstep, and meditate on the Lord's commandments, and wisdom will be given.
readings: Read as the book's wisdom on friendship
6:5–17 is one of the classic passages on friendship in ancient literature, practical about false friends and warm about true ones. Ben Sira returns to the theme in 9:10, 22:19–26 and 37:1–6.
Read as an invitation to take Wisdom's yoke

The yoke of 6:24–31 and its promised rest (6:28) prepare for the book's last invitation (51:23–27) and stand behind the words of Jesus in Matthew 11:28–30. Jewish readers hear in it "the yoke of the Torah" (Mishnah Avot 3:5).

views.C: The lectionary reads 6:5–17 on a weekday of the seventh week in Ordinary Time. The Latin adds "and immortality" to "the medicine of life" (Vulgate 6:16, Douay).
views.O: The Orthodox churches read the Greek of 6:18–37, in which Wisdom's ropes are "threads of blue" and her collar becomes "a robe of glory."
views.P: Protestant readers value the passage as wise counsel and note how Matthew 11:28–30 takes up its language, while holding that Jesus, not Sirach, is the authority behind it.
views.H: The Hebrew of manuscript A and of the Qumran fragment 2Q18 (6:14–15, 20–31) show the poem's Hebrew form, including a pun on musar (6:22) and the "cord of blue" of Numbers 15:38 (6:30). Manuscript A places 27:5–6 after 6:22 and lacks 6:18, 6:23–24, 6:26 and 6:34.
views.J: The Talmud quotes 6:6 (Sanhedrin 100b; Yevamot 63b). The picture of the student clinging to the sages and wearing out their doorstep is close to Mishnah Avot 1:4, and Wisdom's yoke to "the yoke of the Torah" (Mishnah Avot 3:5).

deep.b: Ben Sira's Wisdom asks for the full submission of a working animal or a slave: feet in fetters, neck in a collar, shoulder under a load (6:24–25). Then the picture turns: the fetters become a mighty shelter, the collar a robe of glory, the ropes the blue cord of Israel's tassels, and at the end comes rest (6:28–31). The book closes with the same call: "Bend your neck under the yoke" (51:26). Jesus' words in Matthew 11 follow the same pattern: "Come to me, all of you who are worn out and loaded down, and I myself will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28), and "Lift my yoke onto yourselves and learn from me" (Matthew 11:29). Readers have drawn different conclusions. Some see Jesus speaking deliberately as Wisdom in person, inviting learners to himself instead of to the Torah. Others see a common Jewish image of the yoke of Torah (Mishnah Avot 3:5) and the prophets' promise of rest (Jeremiah 6:16), shared by both teachers without direct borrowing. Either way, Ben Sira shows how Jesus' first hearers would have understood such an invitation: as a teacher's call to take up a discipline that ends in joy.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the blue cord ties Wisdom to the tassels
deep.b: The Hebrew of 6:30, petil tekhelet, is the exact phrase of the law of tassels (Numbers 15:38), which Israelites wore so that they would "remember all the LORD's commands and do them" (Numbers 15:39). If Ben Sira chose the phrase on purpose, Wisdom's "ropes" are the commandments themselves, worn on every Israelite's clothing, and the poem quietly says what 24:23 says openly: Wisdom is the law of Moses. The grandson's Greek "blue thread" keeps the color but loses the link to the tassels.

settings.why: To persuade the young to accept the hard discipline of learning, with the promise that it turns into shelter, glory and rest, and to show them how: stay near the wise and meditate on the commandments.
